props.title: Can We Execute a FlowMind?
props.subtitle: Yes — as of this afternoon. Plus the full prior-art record on pentagon retirement, intent conservation, and the tmux lifecycle.

props.content: This analysis answers five operator questions with evidence, not summaries: a flow.yaml was executed live through the real runtime during the analysis itself, every pentagon reference in the tree was counted, and each claimed failure was re-verified against the current code and classified honestly.

QUESTION 1
props.title: FlowMind execution: proven live, one lane still unconverged
props.subtitle: Not a paper answer — a 24-line community flow was executed through the real runtime during this analysis

props.content:
The `flowmind` CLI is a **compiler by design** — list, show, compile, validate, debug. It never executes. Real execution belongs to `lev exec --flow=<path>`, and that lane turned out to be advertised but unreachable: two independent argument gates each forgot that `--flow` counts as a task. Invoking the CLI's own documented example printed the help screen and **reported success**.

Both gates were fixed during this analysis (one line each), and the demo flow then executed for real: the graph compiled its four nodes, the plan node ran a **live haiku agent through the managed tmux transport to completion**, the execute node ran, and receipts sealed to the canonical per-user data directory. `lev exec --status` showed the run live while it happened.

The run still exits red at the final gate node, and the error is the finding: *"tmux execution must resolve Poly providers through ExecutionBinding, not registry.run."* The gate-evaluator lane is the last piece of the execution path still calling the retired provider-resolution mechanism. That one lane is what stands between today and a fully green flow demo — and it's the same family as the provider-card gap that breaks the flowmind scenario in the dogfood suite.

items.title: Documented invocation prints help, exits 0
items.description: lev exec --flow=<demo> --knob task=... returned the help screen with a success exit code — the first arg gate never counts --flow as work. A script calling this would believe it ran.

items.title: Second gate rejects the same invocation
items.description: Past the help gate, a deeper validation layer threw 'Task description required' — it also forgot --flow. Fixed with the matching one-liner; the error message now names --flow as a valid entry.

items.title: Flow executes: real agent, real receipts
items.description: Graph compiled (4 nodes), plan node ran a live haiku agent via tmux to completion, execute node completed, receipts sealed under the XDG data route with full provenance.

items.title: Gate node fails on the retired resolution path
items.description: The verify gate's evaluator lane still resolves providers through registry.run, which tmux execution forbids. Converging this lane onto ExecutionBinding is the last step to a green end-to-end flow.

props.title: Bonus catch from the live receipts
props.content: The sealed receipt carries execId, runId, and correlationId as three names for the same value — the camelCase identity drift, observed live on the wire. The snake_case rename finished in the last session; the camelCase layer is a queued follow-up lane and this receipt is its concrete exhibit.

props.label: QUESTION 2
props.title: Pentagon: the record disagrees with the memory
props.subtitle: Full census: 2,152 references across 346 files — and what 'hard cutover to core/eval' would actually mean

props.content:
Pentagon is two things wearing one name: the **6-class test taxonomy** (unit, integration, e2e-surface, harness-ratchet, agent-smoke, eval-harness — originally five, hence the shape) and the **per-project proof runner** (`lev pentagon propose/init/run/gate/doctor`) that generates suites, runs them across every surface, and checks proof-log receipts.

The important census finding: **no ruling in the record orders pentagon into core/eval.** The one-brain invariant — core/eval is the only verdict/score/proof *emitter* — was completed and verified in the convergence queue. Pentagon is a verdict *consumer*: a runner and taxonomy, deliberately owned by core/testing, with satellite packages for daemon-surface parity and tmux proof contracts. The closest prior art is a tmux-harness constraint saying proof helpers belong "in core/eval **or core/testing** during migration," and a FlowMind note naming core/eval the consolidation target for sensors, eval suites, and proof projection.

So the operator ruling being made now — *the word pentagon dies* — is new canon, not the completion of an old order. It needs one decision ratified: **where the runner lands.** The recommendation is to absorb it into core/eval (one proof brain: suites, runner, verdict projection under one roof, with the daemon-parity package folding in as daemon-surface suites), accepting the larger rename over preserving a runner-vs-emitter split that mostly exists to justify the extra package.

props.title: Needs your ratification before execution
props.content: Recommended: absorb the proof-runner into core/eval and kill the word everywhere (core first, community/workshop sweep as a follow-up lane). Alternative preserved in the research file: rename in place under core/testing, keeping the runner/emitter separation. Either way the vocabulary dies — the decision is the landing zone.

props.label: QUESTION 3
props.title: Intent conservation: already built, not enforcing
props.subtitle: The DNA literally names it 'the first stock core-loop evaluator' — the work is promotion, not design

props.content:
A complete, tested evaluator pack sits at `core/eval/evaluators/intent_conservation/` — manifest, a measurement flow, a sensor companion, and gate/routing policies — proven loadable by core/eval's own tests. The semantic-control spec locked the rulings in June: semantic control **is the loop mechanism**; the LLM never scores (typed observation goes up, code computes, policy decides); every run seal carries an `intent_ref` with a content hash so mid-loop drift of the intent source itself is detectable; and the verify gate is a slotted template where evaluators attach as lists.

The capture-ledger pattern the project already runs on — compiled intent plus a fidelity score gated at 0.8 — is the human-checkpoint ancestor of the same idea: a preservation score gating a lifecycle edge.

What's missing is enforcement. The pack is wired `warn_only` in exactly one bridge, and the live-runtime failure analysis independently flagged its gate-proof projection as a gap. The recommended landing (pending your confirmation, since the question went unanswered): wire it as the verify gate on the same shell-proof flow this analysis executed, run real executions until conserved/drifted verdicts seal into receipts, then flip the blocking default — an eval-first rollout that also makes the flow demo the first working proof of semantic control.

Intent is L0 ontology; its core-loop manifestation is intent-conservation, the first stock core-loop evaluator. Every run carries intent_ref (+ content hash) as mandatory provenance. — dna/primitives.yaml

props.label: QUESTION 4
props.title: Tmux lifecycle: the SDK exists, the operator surface doesn't
props.subtitle: Nudges, reaper, warm sessions, repair algebra — all built. Reachable by an operator: none of it.

props.content:
The tmux-harness package is a genuinely rich lifecycle SDK. A session object with create/connect/message/capture/wait/observe/shutdown and evidence receipts. An **idle-nudge policy** (threshold, cooldown, max nudges, configurable nudge text) that emits idle-detected/nudge-sent/nudge-exhausted events. A **reaper** with a real outcome algebra — killed, skipped, rebound, resumed, lost, held, escalated — protected-pane guards, and PID-liveness checks. A warm-session registry with stale-session cleanup, session repair (rebind/resume with identity checks), and worker leases with heartbeats.

Two gaps keep all of that invisible. First, **there is no `lev tmux` command group at all** — the CLI even ships a help hint telling users to run `lev tmux kill`, a command that does not exist anywhere. The reaper is reachable only as a package-local script. Second, **nothing schedules the reaper**: the runtime-layers constitution records five independent timer worlds and names the gaps a scheduling substrate must fill — reaper/pollers/health as registered interval providers, unified clock ownership, and the three-clocks policy (readiness, stall, wall-clock budget) for tmux, which is specced but unimplemented.

The team-runtime plan (spawn a tmux-backed worker team, neutral status, clean shutdown, canonical events) stays deferred by your own ruling — it's greenfield, and correctly parked until the lifecycle API underneath it is done.

props.title: Cheapest high-leverage lane in this whole analysis
props.content: lev tmux list / status / kill / reap / nudge as thin handlers over the existing SDK. No new logic — the poly registry auto-discovers handlers, and every one of these operations already has a tested implementation and event vocabulary underneath it.

props.label: QUESTION 5
props.title: Dogfood reds vs. true debt — every claim re-verified at HEAD
props.subtitle: Four items, four different kinds of broken. Two are the product's fault, one is a lying package shape, one is a stale harness. No issue codes — what's actually wrong, in words.

props.title: 🔴 Product bug — fail-closed exit
props.content: One-line semantics change (unobservable exit ≠ success) plus a regression test replaying the real boot-failure capture. Currently held pending an in-flight sweep that rewrites the same files — that hold is worth revisiting.

props.title: 🟠 Packaging debt — finish source-first
props.content: Exports are source-first now and consumers resolve. Remaining: main/types still point at a nonexistent compiled file and a stale compiled tree sits on disk — only matters if the package is ever published.

props.title: 🟡 Stale test — repoint the harness
props.content: Point the community proof harness at the canonical route resolver; core's own reader already does route-first with a labeled historical fallback. The product is emitting evidence correctly.

props.title: 🔴 Missing surface — restore the command
props.content: Thin auto-discovered handler wrapping the existing (healthy, green) readiness-validation library with --json output. The validation logic itself needs zero changes.

props.title: The one that should jump the queue
props.content: The fail-open exit code is a truth-integrity defect in the run ledger — the exact machinery every receipt, eval, and future intent-conservation verdict depends on. Its fix is deliberately on hold behind an in-flight classification sweep; that hold is a judgment call worth revisiting now that the convergence queue is done.
